rv.q: Barry Manilow and Bruce Sussman's musical about the Comedian Harmonists, a German singing group that was torn apart by the Nazis, is deeply sincere but dramatically inert.
They make no false steps in Danny and the Deep Blue Sea, and we follow wherever they might lead.
Bruce Sussman and Barry Manilow’s conventional new musical does a rudimentary but essential job of reviving a dead historical act.
As an act, though, the group lacks the intrinsic appeal that might sustain our interest through song after song.
The show — basically a fable — doesn’t meet the moment as much as the moment crashes over it.
That’s the central takeaway of “Harmony”: not everything is harmonious, but nonetheless there is much that’s worth listening to.
It's fascinating to learn about the Comedian Harmonists, and this is material ripe for musical theatre treatment.
Timely it may sadly be, but a theatrical triumph it still isn’t.

As enjoyable and affecting as Harmony is—and as timely, with antisemitism on the rise worldwide—it doesn't make the case that, among all that we must never forget, the Comedian Harmonists merit quite this degree of remembrance.
Neither the guys nor the grim and eventually bludgeoning show have a gift for levity.
The play, equal parts glitzy and superficial, consists largely of jaunty songs, written by Manilow, that the group sings on stages — including Carnegie Hall — as they travel the world.
Mostly, though, the show is a maudlin affair, even before it starts to pull the Harmonists apart.
Nonetheless, I’m reviving it for Harmony, the superb new musical for which Barry Manilow wrote the tunes and Bruce Sussman wrote the lyrics and book.
Harmony is an altogether original and serious work that beautifully marries the story of the Comedian Harmonists with that of the years of their rise and fall.
Certainly, the musical concludes with notes, literal and figurative, of warmth and hope, reminding us that harmony can be achieved not just by different musical parts but among different people.
Harmony successfully melds comedy & drama and history & entertainment.
Flaws and all, and despite its rocky road to Broadway, Harmony is ultimately a rewarding experience, a feisty/funny survivor which remains tragically timely.

Indeed. as the Nazis rise to power grows and the group’s “harmony” and livelihood are increasingly threatened – the words “Heil Hitler” have never felt more chilling to me – we feel the fear that these men did for both their livelihood and their lives.
This is a show that my grandparents would have raved about during the post-services Kiddush luncheon: undeniably moving and extremely powerful, the pros of Harmony generally outweigh the cons.
The morose story mixed with Manilow’s characteristic earworm melodies leaves audiences humming at times, and tearing up at others.
The show feels now like an occasionally enjoyable entertainment more than something we need to see.

Unfortunately, “Harmony” contains a weak score, with surprisingly generic and bland music by Manilow (none of which stands up to his wonderfully catchy pop hits), and pedestrian lyrics by Sussman (who also wrote the comparatively stronger book).
Being such an awesome harmonist, Manilow imbues the songs with enormous spirit.
Harmony will continue to sing out in the minds of audiences long after they leave the theater, too.
There was little specificity in its construct.
Yet the searching depth of this finale cannot make up for a broadly unfulfilling work.
Harmony finally arrives on Broadway after 25 years in the making, and its cast, music, and poignant yet thoroughly entertaining story make it worth the wait.
“Harmony” doesn’t always serve that memory well.

The unevenly staged Harmony is a shakily constructed set of misfiring elements, whose most compelling beats around Nazism, antisemitism, and bigotry—all points resoundingly and rightly made—feel imposed and didactic rather than flowing naturally from the source material.
Harmony looked Broadway bound from the start; it had to overcome many obstacles and, while still saddled with imperfections, unquestionably deserves to be there.
And now he’s written a musical that will make the world remember.
Now thanks to Harmony: A New Musical, written by the legendary Barry Manilow and his longtime collaborator Bruce Sussman their story lives again.

cn.t: Critics give mixed reviews to Manilow and Sussman's long-gestating musical about the Comedian Harmonists, praising its timely story and heartfelt performances but citing structural flaws, pacing issues, and a weak first act that improves considerably in Act Two.

vs.sum: The Ethel Barrymore Theatre offers good sightlines with a well-raked mezzanine and minimal obstructions, though some box seats have limited views. Sound quality is average, with some reports of less than ideal acoustics. Comfort is typical for a Broadway theater, with decent legroom in some areas. However, facilities are lacking, with only one restroom on the lower level leading to potential congestion.

acc.note: 5 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No steps from sidewalk. Infrared devices available.

vr.q: For me, it is my favourite musical of the season so far, and I definitely think it will be in contention for that best musical race!
